transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah… honestly, the thing that finally made me come in is how tense my body has gotten. My shoulders and neck are just clenched all day, like I’m bracing myself constantly — almost like there’s a classroom observation going on that never ends, even when nothing is actually happening. I teach preschool, so I’m used to being “on,” you know, but this feels different.

By the end of the day my jaw aches too, like I’ve been holding it tight for hours without realizing. And I play guitar in the evenings, or I try to, because that’s usually something I enjoy, but lately my jaw and neck are so tight and sore that I can hardly even relax into it. It’s embarrassing in a way, because it sounds like just tension, but it’s constant enough that it’s really wearing me down.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn't a specific reason for it, or feeling anxious in situations where you wouldn't expect to be?

Yes. Very much, actually. It’s like my mind doesn’t need a real, immediate problem to latch onto — it just starts circling.

I’ll think about whether I’m ever going to get hired again, even if there’s no new reason that day to be thinking about that. Then it turns into, “Have I ruined my reputation with the parents?” and I start replaying little conversations or moments, wondering if someone interpreted something the wrong way. Then it jumps to bigger things, like retirement — like, “Is that slipping away now? Did I mess up the stability I was supposed to have at this age?”

And then it gets… honestly kind of extreme, but it feels real in the moment. Like if I make some small mistake during a story-time activity — maybe I mix up the order of something or don’t handle a transition perfectly — my brain will go, “See, maybe you shouldn’t be trusted with children.” Which sounds awful to say out loud, because logically I know one small mistake shouldn’t mean that. But the worry doesn’t stay logical. It just keeps expanding, and I have a hard time getting it to stop.
Do you find that your worrying happens more days than not and feels excessive, even when you try to control it?

Yes… more days than not, definitely. It feels excessive, even when I can see that from the outside it probably sounds like I’m taking one thought and building a whole disaster around it.

It’s like my mind keeps circling and circling. I’ll start with, “What if I never get hired again?” and then it turns into, “What if the parents think badly of me now?” or “What if I’ve ruined my reputation?” Then somehow I’m thinking about retirement, like whether that stability is slipping away, and whether I’ve somehow thrown off the whole rest of my life.

And it doesn’t stop there. I can make one small mistake during a story-time activity — something that should be normal, like mixing up the order of a book or not handling a moment perfectly — and my brain goes straight to, “Maybe this means I shouldn’t be trusted with children.” I hate even saying that because it sounds so harsh and unreasonable, but in the moment it feels like a real possibility.

I do try to control it. I try to reason with myself, or tell myself I’m overreacting, but it just keeps finding another angle. It’s exhausting.
Has this constant worrying and tension started to interfere with your daily life, like making it harder to focus on work, enjoy your guitar playing, or even get through the day comfortably?

Yes… it has, more than I wanted to admit at first. It’s not just that I feel worried internally — it’s actually getting in the way of me doing the things I need to do to get back into a classroom.

I’ve missed application deadlines because I’ll open the application and start second-guessing every part of it — the wording, the references, whether the school will already have heard something negative about me — and then I put it off “just for tonight,” and suddenly the deadline is gone. And interviews have been rough. I’ll prepare, sometimes too much, but then when I’m actually sitting there I stumble through answers because I’m trying to read everyone’s faces and guess what they’re thinking about me.

Even with story-time, which used to be something I felt really comfortable with, I’ve stopped volunteering for it unless someone else handles the planning. I used to be the person who’d jump in and say, “Sure, I can do that,” but now if I’m responsible for choosing the book or structuring the activity, I start worrying I’ll mess it up or it’ll reflect badly on me. So I hang back.

So, yes — it’s interfering. It’s keeping me from getting back into the classroom in any reliable way, and that’s… that’s hard to say, because teaching is the thing I’m supposed to know how to do.
Have you noticed any other physical symptoms, like stomach issues, headaches, or dizziness, that don’t seem to have a clear medical explanation?

I’m not really sure. I don’t want to say yes just to say yes, because I haven’t noticed a clear pattern like, “Every time I worry, I get stomach pain,” or anything that definite.

I mean, I do feel worn down a lot, but in terms of specific things like headaches or dizziness or stomach problems… I can’t honestly point to something and say, “That’s definitely happening and there’s no medical reason for it.” I may just not be paying close enough attention, because most of what I notice is the worrying itself and how much time it takes up in my head.

So… I guess my answer is I haven’t really noticed those kinds of physical symptoms in a clear way.
Have you been feeling fatigued or experiencing a lack of energy nearly every day, even if it’s not clear why?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean… I do feel tired a lot, but I don’t know if I would say it’s nearly every day in the way you’re asking, or if it’s more that I feel mentally worn out from being in my head so much.

It’s hard for me to separate “lack of energy” from just feeling drained after worrying, if that makes sense. Like, I’ll get through part of the day and then feel like I’ve already used up all my capacity, but I can’t point to it and say, “Yes, this is a constant fatigue with no clear reason.” I’m not sure I’ve been tracking it that carefully.

So I guess… I’ve noticed feeling depleted, but I don’t know that I can clearly say it’s nearly every day or that it’s this separate physical lack of energy.
Have you had trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even when you’re tired?

Yes. That one I can answer more clearly.

Most nights, even when I’m genuinely tired, I’ll get into bed and it’s like my mind decides that’s the time to start reviewing everything. I’ll replay interview answers — things I said, things I should have said differently, whether I sounded nervous or unprepared. Then it’ll shift to bills, or licensing forms, or some detail I’m worried I forgot, and I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just think it through once so you can let it go,” but it doesn’t really work that way. It turns into hours of going over the same things.

And then even when I do fall asleep, I often wake up around four in the morning. Not just waking up and rolling over — I wake up already tense, like my body is bracing for the day before the day has even started. I’ll immediately start calculating what could go wrong, what I need to fix, what I’m behind on. By then it’s hard to get back to sleep because my head is already moving.

So yes, falling asleep and staying asleep have both been a problem.
Do you often feel irritable, restless, or like you can't relax, as if you're always 'keyed up'?

Yes… definitely. I think that’s actually one of the clearest things for me.

Honestly, what finally pushed me to come in is that my shoulders and neck feel clenched almost all day. It’s like I’m bracing for something constantly — like I’m waiting for a classroom observation that never ends, if that makes sense. Even when nothing is actively happening, my body feels like it’s preparing for being judged or caught off guard.

And it isn’t just a little stiffness. By the end of the day my jaw aches from holding it tight, and I notice it especially when I try to do something normal and enjoyable, like playing guitar. I’ll sit down thinking it’ll help me unwind, but my jaw and neck are so tight that I can barely enjoy it. I have to remind myself to unclench, and then a minute later I’m clenched again.

So yes, I’d say I feel keyed up. Maybe I don’t always notice it emotionally right away, but my body is doing it all day.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about physical symptoms you're experiencing, like your muscle tension or jaw pain, to the point where the worry itself becomes a big source of stress?

Yes, but… I think it’s less that I’m worried the jaw pain itself is something dangerous, if that’s what you mean. It’s more that the physical tension becomes another thing my mind uses as proof that I’m not okay, or that I’m not handling things the way I should.

Like, I’ll notice my jaw is tight or my neck is locked up, and then instead of just thinking, “Oh, I’m tense,” my mind jumps into this whole chain. It starts with, “Why can’t I relax?” and then somehow I’m back to worrying about whether I’ll ever get hired again, whether I’ve damaged my reputation with parents, whether people see me as unreliable or not safe to trust. And then it widens out even more — retirement, money, whether I’m falling behind in a way I won’t be able to recover from.

And the part that feels embarrassing to say out loud is that sometimes it attaches to very small things. Like if I made one small mistake during a story-time activity, or I stumbled over something, or didn’t handle a moment exactly right, I’ll start thinking, “Does that mean I shouldn’t be trusted with children?” Which sounds extreme when I say it here, but in my head it doesn’t feel extreme at the time. It feels like I’m trying to prevent something terrible by thinking it through from every angle.

So yes, the muscle tension and jaw pain add stress, but mostly because they feed into this bigger loop where I keep questioning my competence, my future, my reputation — everything, really.

Have you ever found yourself extremely anxious or preoccupied about a physical symptom, like your muscle tension or jaw pain, even when doctors or others have told you there isn’t a serious medical issue causing it?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, exactly.

I don’t think I’ve had a doctor tell me, “There’s definitely nothing medically wrong,” and then I kept obsessing that there must be anyway. At least, that’s not how it feels to me. With the jaw and neck tension, I’m not usually thinking, “This is some hidden disease” or “They missed something serious.” It’s more that I notice the tension and then I get upset by what it seems to say about me — like I’m not coping, or I can’t calm myself down, or I’m somehow failing at being a normal functioning person.

So… I guess no, not in the sense of being convinced there’s a serious medical cause after being reassured. It’s more that the symptom becomes part of the worry loop. But I don’t think I’m especially preoccupied with the medical explanation itself.

So… I guess no, not in the sense of being convinced there’s a serious medical cause after being reassured. It’s more that the symptom becomes part of the worry loop. But I don’t think I’m especially preoccupied with the medical explanation itself.

Other candidates (F43.22, F45.8, F48.8) are ruled out due to insufficient evidence of adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) given the chronic and pervasive nature of symptoms rather than a specific stressor; no clear evidence of a somatic symptom disorder (F45.8); and insufficient evidence of other specified anxiety disorders (F48.8) given the clear pattern of GAD.
